title: DPE Entry 2.0
description: One Data Protection Exposure: a named class of fault in how a system handles personal data. An entry describes the fault itself, the way CWE describes a class of weakness. It names no organisation, no product and no site. Whether a given deployment exhibits it is for a researcher to establish and publish; the registry only defines the fault, how to detect it, what would refute it, and which provisions it engages. Explicitly for faults that are not vulnerabilities: nothing is exploitable, the system works as designed, and the design is the problem. Firmware phoning home to a third country, an SDK uploading a contact list, a television reporting what is on screen: none of these get a CVE, and until now there was no number to cite for them.

id.description: Permanent identifier. Never reused, never deleted. A deprecated entry keeps its number and its URL.

name.description: The citable unit. One word, memorable, in English, describing the behaviour of the system and not the harm to the person. Heartbleed, not CVE-2014-0160. Never reused, even after deprecation.

family.description: Coarse grouping so the catalogue stays navigable. Not a severity and not a judgement.

summary.description: One sentence, in terms of the mechanism. This is what people will quote.

status.description: draft: proposed, not yet accepted. active: in use. superseded: replaced by a better-defined entry, see supersededBy. deprecated: no longer considered a distinct fault; kept online with the reason.

why_it_matters.description: What it costs the person whose data it is. Concrete, not abstract.

common_causes.description: Typical origins, described generically: 'tag hardcoded outside the consent gate', never a vendor name.

not_this.description: The neighbouring fault it is most often confused with, and the dividing line. Sharp boundaries are what keep an entry usable in a dispute.

detection.description: How to establish it without exploiting anything, the way a vulnerability scanner confirms a CVE by finding a deterministic indicator.

indicator.description: The concrete thing that settles it. Must be checkable without interpretation.

qod.description: Quality of detection of the method, not the seriousness of the fault.

capture_requirements.description: Conditions the measurement must meet, e.g. clean profile, no interaction, separate capture per consent mode. A capture that fails these produces a confident wrong answer.

attribution.description: Acceptable ways to attribute the behaviour. Referer is never acceptable: it is spoofable and instrumentation spoofs it.

falsifiers.description: What would refute a claim that this fault is present. Mandatory, and the reason an entry survives contest: a researcher who works through this list before publishing cannot be caught out by the obvious objection.

checkable.description: not-from-capture means it cannot be settled from the recording alone and needs context the researcher must supply.

does_not_establish.description: Explicit limits, so they travel with every use of this entry. Unlawfulness is always on this list: that is for a supervisory authority or a court.

reproduction.description: At least one route that needs no tooling owned by the registry.

public_scanners.description: Third-party services that can confirm this fault with a permanent result URL, so a researcher can point at a measurement that is not their own.

legal.description: Which provisions the fault engages. Per jurisdiction, so the entry is usable outside one country: the behaviour is the same across the EEA and only the citation differs.

items.description: Id of a file in law/.
Id of a file in caselaw/.

rebuttals.description: The objections a researcher will meet, with the answer. Written once here instead of in every article.

seen_in_the_wild.description: That the fault occurs in practice, without naming anyone. The registry defines faults; who exhibits one is for a researcher to establish and publish under their own name. References here point at published research, never at an unpublished measurement.

credit.description: Who proposed and refined this entry. Permanent, because attribution is what a contributor gets in return.

changes.description: Append-only. Definitions shift as the field learns, and an entry that changed meaning in 2028 must still be readable as what it meant in 2026.

applies_to.description: Which kinds of system this fault can occur in. A fault is not tied to a technology: consent that cannot be refused looks different on a television than in a browser, but it is the same fault.

not_a_vulnerability.description: Why this is not a security vulnerability, stated so nobody files it in the wrong place. Usually: nothing is exploitable, the behaviour is intended by the builder, and the objection is to the design rather than to a defect in it.
